Key ideas

Analysing motion through graphs

Definitions

Origin: the initial point from where a body moves
Acceleration: the rate of change of velocity
Gradient: the slope of a graph. The gradient of a straight line can be calculated as the rise divided by the run.

Formulas

Average velocity
vav=ΔsΔtv_{\text{av}} = \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}vav​=ΔtΔs​
vavv_{\text{av}}vav​Average velocity (m s−1\mathrm{\text{m\,s}^{-1}}ms−1)Δs\Delta sΔsChange in displacement (m\mathrm{m}m)Δt\Delta tΔtChange in time (s\mathrm{s}s)
Average speed
average speed=ΔdΔt\text{average speed} = \frac{\Delta d}{\Delta t}average speed=ΔtΔd​
Δd\Delta dΔdChange in distance (m\mathrm{m}m)Δt\Delta tΔtChange in time (s\mathrm{s}s)

7B

New knowledgeThe vector quantities of motion

Analysing motion through graphs

Understanding how to analyse motion in a straight line is the starting point for analysing all motion.

The analysis of motion is extensively used in a range of different fields such as flight, racing car driving and even for video umpires in sports.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 175
7B

New knowledgeDistance versus displacement

Analysing motion through graphs

Imagine a hiker who walks from camp A to camp B.

The camps are separated by a distance of 10 km when you travel directly east.

However, it is impossible for the hiker to go directly east, as a steep mountain blocks the path.

Therefore, to get to camp B, the hiker must walk a distance of 11.7 km around the mountain.

Figure 7B–7 Example of a hike with a displacement of 10 km and a distance of 11.7 km
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 176
7B

New knowledgeDistance versus displacement

Analysing motion through graphs

This example highlights the difference between distance and displacement.

Displacement is the direct distance from one point to another.

Displacement is a vector quantity and therefore requires both a magnitude and a direction.

When the hiker has reached camp B, their displacement from the origin (starting position) is 10 km east.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 177
7B

New knowledgeDistance versus displacement

Analysing motion through graphs

You know that the hiker actually travelled 11.7 km in order to reach camp B; which is a measure of distance and is a scalar quantity so it requires a magnitude only.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 178
7B

New knowledgeSpeed versus velocity

Analysing motion through graphs

Velocity is the rate of change of displacement.

It is a vector quantity because it requires both a magnitude and direction.

The direction of the velocity is the same as the direction of the change in displacement.

In motion, the velocity can be either positive or negative.

Figure 7B–8 Conversion between kilometres per hour and metres per second
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 189
7B

New knowledgeSpeed versus velocity

Analysing motion through graphs

For example, if a velocity of 10 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1 north means that every second you are moving 10 m further north away from your starting position.

The greater the velocity, the faster you are moving from the starting position.

Speed is the rate of change of distance.

This is a scalar quantity and therefore only requires a magnitude.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 1810
7B

New knowledgeSpeed versus velocity

Analysing motion through graphs

The formula for speed is very similar to the formula for velocity, the two are shown side by side for comparison below.

Speed is often given in terms of kilometres per hour (km h−1\text{km h}^{-1}km h−1) as many vehicles use this as a measure of their speed.

When given a value of speed or velocity in terms of kilometres per hour, it is useful to convert it immediately into metres per second.

This can be done by dividing the km h−1\text{km h}^{-1}km h−1 value by 3.6.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 1811
7B

New knowledgeSpeed versus velocity

Analysing motion through graphs

So, to convert from m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1 to km h−1\text{km h}^{-1}km h−1, multiply the m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1 value by 3.6 as shown in the figure below.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 1812
7B

New knowledgeAcceleration

Analysing motion through graphs

Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.

It is given the symbol aaa.

The SI unit for acceleration is metres per second per second (m s−2\text{m s}^{-2}m s−2).

Imagine a car, starting from rest and travelling in a straight line, that is accelerating at 4 m s−2\text{m s}^{-2}m s−2; by the end of the first second that car will be travelling with a velocity of 4 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 1913
7B

New knowledgeAcceleration

Analysing motion through graphs

When 2 seconds have passed, the car would have gained another 4 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1 to its velocity and will be travelling at 8 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 1914
7B

New knowledgeDisplacement–time graphs

Analysing motion through graphs

Displacement–time graphs display how far an object is away from its origin at a given point in time.

This can be shown by the displacement–time graph of a person going for a jog in Figure 7B–10.

The jogger leaves their origin, their house, and runs away from their house for 20 s, covering a distance of 80 m.

The jogger then stops and rests for 24 s before turning around and running the 80 m back towards their house in 12 s.

Figure 7B–10 The displacement–time graph of a jogger
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 1915
7B

New knowledgeDisplacement–time graphs

Analysing motion through graphs

The jogger then continues to run in the opposite direction, away from their house, and covers another 80 m in 20 s.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 1916
7B

New knowledgeGradient of a displacement–time graph

Analysing motion through graphs

There are a few useful principles that can be applied to all graphs.

Many questions will ask about the gradient of the line of best fit.

The gradient of the graph is given by: gradient=riserun\text{gradient} = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}gradient=runrise​ The gradient gives useful information; for example, the gradient of a displacement–time graph gives the velocity of the object.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 2017
7B

New knowledgeDisplacement–time and velocity–time graphs compared

Analysing motion through graphs

The gradient of the graph can be thought of as the steepness of the graph, it is often important to be able to quickly assess the gradient of any graph.

Consider the motion of a body displayed on the displacement–time graph in Figure 7B–11 on the next page. 1 From A to B, the steepness is positive and constant, giving a constant positive gradient and therefore velocity. 2 The section B to C is steeper than the previous section (A–B), but it is still constant and positive, giving a constant positive gradient (velocity). 3 Section C to D is flat and as it has no incline, the gradient and therefore the velocity is zero during this time. 4 The steepness of the segment D to E is negative, quite steep and constant.

This gives a large, constant, negative gradient (velocity).

To graph the velocity–time graph of the body, we would have to graph the value of the gradient of the displacement–time graph at each point.

Figure 7B–11 The displacement–time graph of a body moving in a straight line with a variety of different velocities
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 2118
7B

New knowledgeDisplacement–time and velocity–time graphs compared

Analysing motion through graphs

This is shown in Figure 7B–12.

The two graphs are positioned so the points A–E are vertically aligned in both graphs. 1 From A to B the gradient in the top graph is 1 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1, as shown in the bottom graph.

The dashed vertical line in the bottom graph indicates that the velocity change was instant.

With most physical objects this is unrealistic but that can be ignored here. 2 From B to C the gradient in the top graph is 2 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1. 3 From C to D the gradient in the top graph is 0 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1, so the body is stationary. 4 From D to E the gradient is –3, and the negative sign indicates the body has changed direction and is returning to its starting position.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 2119
7B

New knowledgeDisplacement–time and velocity–time graphs compared

Analysing motion through graphs

Its final displacement is zero..

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 2120
7B

New knowledgeVelocity–time graphs

Analysing motion through graphs

Velocity–time graphs display the velocity of an object at a given point in time.

This can be demonstrated by the velocity–time graph in below for a car doing a U-turn at a set of traffic lights.

The car takes 50 s to uniformly accelerate to a speed of 15 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1.

The car then travels at a constant velocity of 15 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1 for 100 s.

Figure 7B–13 The velocity–time graph of a car doing a U-turn at a set of traffic lights on a straight stretch of road
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 2421
7B

New knowledgeVelocity–time graphs

Analysing motion through graphs

The driver, seeing the traffic lights on red, brakes and the car takes 20 s to decelerate to a velocity of zero.

The car remains stationary at the lights for 30 s.

Then the light turns green and the car does a U-turn and accelerates for 50 s in the opposite direction to which it was originally travelling.

This is why the velocity has become negative.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 2422
7B

New knowledgeVelocity–time graphs

Analysing motion through graphs

The car then maintains a constant velocity of 10 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1 for 50 s.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 2423
7B

New knowledgeGradient of a velocity–time graph

Analysing motion through graphs

On a velocity–time graph, the velocity is on the yyy-axis and time is on the xxx-axis.

The gradient of the line represents the acceleration because gradient=riserun=ΔvΔt=a\text{gradient} = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = agradient=runrise​=ΔtΔv​=a.

Dividing m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1 by seconds, you get the unit m s−1s=m s−2\frac{\text{m s}^{-1}}{\text{s}} = \text{m s}^{-2}sm s−1​=m s−2.

You may hear this spoken as ‘metres per second per second’.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 2424
7B

New knowledgeThe area under a velocity–time graph

Analysing motion through graphs

The area under a velocity–time graph represents the change in displacement.

Consider the velocity–time graph of a hiker, walking with a constant straight-line velocity of 1 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1 for 5 seconds (Figure 7B–14).

The change in displacement of the hiker after 5 seconds can be determined by finding the area under the graph: area=s=vt=(1)(5)=5\text{area} = s = vt = (1)(5) = 5area=s=vt=(1)(5)=5 m For non-constant velocity, the change in displacement is still found using the area under the velocity–time graph, as shown in Figure 7B–15.

The unit is given by multiplying the xxx-axis unit with the yyy-axis unit as shown, m×s−1×s=m\text{m} \times \text{s}^{-1} \times \text{s} = \text{m}m×s−1×s=m.

Figure 7B–14 The velocity–time graph of a hiker walking at 1 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ for 5 seconds
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 2625
7B

New knowledgeAcceleration–time graphs

Analysing motion through graphs

Acceleration-time graphs display the acceleration of an object at a given point in time.

This can be demonstrated by the acceleration–time graph of a car travelling east that is braking as it comes up to a stop sign.

As seen in the acceleration–time graph in Figure 7B–16, when the car brakes, it accelerates at a constant rate of −4 m s−2\text{m s}^{-2}m s−2 for 6 s.

The negative value means that the car is accelerating in the west direction and therefore the velocity of the car is being reduced.

Figure 7B–16 Acceleration–time graph of a car braking as it approaches a stop sign
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 2926
7B

New knowledgeAcceleration–time graphs

Analysing motion through graphs

The car then remains stationary at the lights for 4 s before accelerating uniformly by 3 m s−2\text{m s}^{-2}m s−2.

Even though the car’s acceleration was directed west for the first 6 seconds, the car did not travel west through its entire journey.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 2927
7B

New knowledgeThe area under an acceleration–time graph

Analysing motion through graphs

In an acceleration–time graph, acceleration, aaa, is on the yyy-axis and time, ttt, is on the xxx-axis.

The area under an acceleration–time graph is the change in velocity as: area=Δv=at\text{area} = \Delta v = atarea=Δv=at For non-constant acceleration, the change in velocity is still found using the area under the acceleration–time graph.

The unit is given by multiplying the units on the xxx and yyy-axis together to give m s−2×s=m s−1\text{m s}^{-2} \times \text{s} = \text{m s}^{-1}m s−2×s=m s−1.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 2928
7B

New knowledgeInstantaneous velocity versus average velocity

Analysing motion through graphs

Speed and velocity can be either instantaneous or average.

Imagine a truck is moving down a straight road.

A displacement–time graph of the truck’s motion is shown in Figure 7B–17.

The gradient of this line will be the velocity because: gradient=riserun=ΔsΔt=v\text{gradient} = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t} = vgradient=runrise​=ΔtΔs​=v But the gradient changes after 6 seconds and the line becomes steeper, indicating an increase in velocity.

Figure 7B–17 Displacement–time graph of a truck driving along a road
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 3229
7B

New knowledgeInstantaneous velocity versus average velocity

Analysing motion through graphs

This means that the velocity for the first 6 seconds is: vav=ΔsΔt=20−06−0=3.33v_{\text{av}} = \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t} = \frac{20 - 0}{6 - 0} = 3.33vav​=ΔtΔs​=6−020−0​=3.33 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1 The velocity for the next 4 seconds is: vav=ΔsΔt=80−2010−6=15v_{\text{av}} = \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t} = \frac{80 - 20}{10 - 6} = 15vav​=ΔtΔs​=10−680−20​=15 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1 The average velocity for the whole 10-second trip is: vav=ΔsΔt=80−010−0=8v_{\text{av}} = \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t} = \frac{80 - 0}{10 - 0} = 8vav​=ΔtΔs​=10−080−0​=8 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1 The formula for average speed and velocity must be used with care.

As you can see from Figure 7B–17, considering different parts of the graph will give different results as the velocity of the object changes.

You should remember that this formula gives the average velocity of a body and should not be confused with a formula that gives the final velocity.

Measuring instantaneous velocity is much more difficult.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 3230
7B

New knowledgeInstantaneous velocity versus average velocity

Analysing motion through graphs

In fact, any real-world measurement of velocity will always be an average because it is calculated by dividing the distance travelled by the time that it took the body to travel that distance.

As the time interval approaches zero, the velocity becomes closer to the instantaneous velocity.

For example, imagine a car that is accelerating and therefore its velocity is constantly increasing.

The displacement–time graph for the accelerating car is shown in Figure 7B–18.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 3231
7B

New knowledgeInstantaneous velocity versus average velocity

Analysing motion through graphs

As the gradient is constantly changing, the velocity is also constantly changing.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 3232

We doDistance and displacement

Analysing motion through graphs
A track runner is running around a circular track that has a circumference of 500 m. The runner does exactly four laps, finishing where they started.
a Calculate the distance travelled by the runner.
b Calculate the displacement of the runner once they complete one full lap.
Key idea · Average velocityvav=ΔsΔtv_{\text{av}} = \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}vav​=ΔtΔs​

Working

a 500×4=2000500 \times 4 = 2000500×4=2000 m
b Since the runner finishes where they start, they will have zero net displacement because they have not moved relative to the origin.
a 2000 m; b zero
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 18, Worked example 7B-142
7B

We doDisplacement–time graph gradient

Analysing motion through graphs
A body moves from rest in a straight line. Its motion is displayed in the displacement–time graph (right).
What is the gradient of the graph? Include a unit in your answer and state what the gradient represents.
Key idea · Average velocityvav=ΔsΔtv_{\text{av}} = \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}vav​=ΔtΔs​

Working

The first step in determining the gradient of a graph is to take two clear points from the line, determine the rise and the run and then divide the rise by the run.
gradient=riserun\text{gradient} = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}gradient=runrise​
=8−24−1= \frac{8 - 2}{4 - 1}=4−18−2​
=2= 2=2
As you are dividing the values on the yyy-axis (rise) by the values of the xxx-axis (run), the gradient represents the velocity as v=ΔdΔtv = \frac{\Delta d}{\Delta t}v=ΔtΔd​. The unit for this graph is ms=m s−1\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}} = \text{m s}^{-1}sm​=m s−1.
2 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1; the gradient is the velocity
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 20, Worked example 7B-243
7B

We doReading a velocity–time graph

Analysing motion through graphs
A ball is thrown vertically into the air and it leaves the thrower’s hand at an initial velocity of 10 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1. The velocity–time graph of the ball from the moment it leaves the thrower’s hand is shown below (air resistance is ignored).
a When the velocity of the ball is zero, the time is 1.02 s. In terms of the ball’s height, what is the significance of when the velocity is zero?
b Calculate the gradient of the line and comment on the significance of this gradient.
Key idea · Average velocityvav=ΔsΔtv_{\text{av}} = \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}vav​=ΔtΔs​

Working

a When the velocity of the ball is zero, the ball will be at its maximum height.
b gradient=riserun\text{gradient} = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}gradient=runrise​
=0−101.02−0= \frac{0 - 10}{1.02 - 0}=1.02−00−10​
=−9.8= -9.8=−9.8 m s−2\text{m s}^{-2}m s−2
This gradient is the acceleration due to gravity.
Note that the acceleration is changing the velocity. As seen above, the velocity has gone from being positive to zero to negative.
a maximum height; b −9.8 m s−2\text{m s}^{-2}m s−2, the acceleration due to gravity
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 25, Worked example 7B-344
7B

We doArea under a velocity–time graph

Analysing motion through graphs
A cyclist rides north up a straight road, turns around and then returns to where they started. A velocity–time graph of this situation is shown below.
a Find the displacement of the cyclist once they have travelled for 120 s.
b What is the displacement after 180 s?
c What is the total distance covered after 180 s?
Key idea · Average velocityvav=ΔsΔtv_{\text{av}} = \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}vav​=ΔtΔs​

Working

a The displacement is the area under the graph. To find the area under the graph, divide the graph into a series of triangles and rectangles as shown on the next page.
The area under the graph up to 120 s, and therefore the displacement, can then be found by adding the area of all the shapes:
12(20)(5)+(60)(5)+12(40)(5)=450\frac{1}{2}(20)(5) + (60)(5) + \frac{1}{2}(40)(5) = 45021​(20)(5)+(60)(5)+21​(40)(5)=450 m
As this question asked for displacement (a vector quantity), a direction is required. The direction is north.
b Note that this graph has a negative value for velocity; this indicates that the cyclist is travelling south. To calculate the displacement after 180 s, the graph needs to be divided into a rectangle and triangles as shown below.
The important point to remember is that when calculating the displacement, the negative value for velocity needs to be considered. Therefore, the area for the blue triangle is:
area=12(60)(−15)\text{area} = \frac{1}{2}(60)(-15)area=21​(60)(−15)
=−450= -450=−450 m
The negative does not indicate negative area but rather the direction travelled: south. Therefore, the total displacement of the bike after 180 s is:
450+−450=0450 + -450 = 0450+−450=0 m
c Distance is a scalar quantity. Therefore, no direction is required. This means that any negative velocities must be turned into positive values. This is because in the first 120 s the cyclist travels 450 m, and from 120 s to 180 s the cyclist travels another 450 m. This gives a total distance covered of 900 m.
a 450 m north; b 0 m; c 900 m
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 27, Worked example 7B-445
7B

We doArea under an acceleration–time graph

Analysing motion through graphs
A car, initially travelling at 72 km h−1\text{km h}^{-1}km h−1, is travelling on a straight road when it approaches to some roadworks. The car slows to the new speed limit and then accelerates again once it has passed the roadworks. The acceleration–time graph of the car’s journey is shown below.
a Calculate the speed that the car travelled past the roadworks in kilometres per hour.
b Calculate the speed, in km h−1\text{km h}^{-1}km h−1, of the car at the end of the 50 s.
Key idea · Average velocityvav=ΔsΔtv_{\text{av}} = \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}vav​=ΔtΔs​

Working

a The first step is to interpret this diagram. The car is accelerating at a rate of −1 m s−2\text{m s}^{-2}m s−2 for 8 s as it approaches the roadworks. The car is passing through the roadworks at a constant velocity (as there is no acceleration) from 8 s to 42 s. After 42 s, the car has left the roadworks and accelerates. Therefore:
initial velocity of the car =723.6= \frac{72}{3.6}=3.672​ =20= 20=20 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1
change in velocity = area under the graph =(−1)(8)= (-1)(8)=(−1)(8) =−8= -8=−8 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1
final velocity =20−8= 20 - 8=20−8 =12= 12=12 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1
convert m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1 to km h−1\text{km h}^{-1}km h−1 =(12)(3.6)= (12)(3.6)=(12)(3.6) =43.2= 43.2=43.2 km h−1\text{km h}^{-1}km h−1
b Since you know from part a that the car will be travelling at 12 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1 after 42 s, you only need to consider the change in velocity after this point.
change in velocity of the car = area under the graph =(2)(8)= (2)(8)=(2)(8) =16= 16=16 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1
final velocity =12+16= 12 + 16=12+16 =28= 28=28 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1
convert m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1 to km h−1\text{km h}^{-1}km h−1 =(28)(3.6)= (28)(3.6)=(28)(3.6) =101= 101=101 km h−1\text{km h}^{-1}km h−1
a 43.2 km h−1\text{km h}^{-1}km h−1; b 101 km h−1\text{km h}^{-1}km h−1
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 30, Worked example 7B-546
7B

We doAverage velocity and the instantaneous velocity

Analysing motion through graphs
What is the difference between the average velocity and the instantaneous velocity? Use Figure 7B–18 to help answer your question.
Key idea · Average velocityvav=ΔsΔtv_{\text{av}} = \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}vav​=ΔtΔs​

Working

The average velocity of an object is the change in the displacement of an object divided by the time. The instantaneous velocity of an object is the velocity of an object at a specific point in time.
In Figure 7B–18 the average velocity is:
v=ΔsΔt=128−08−0=16v = \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t} = \frac{128 - 0}{8 - 0} = 16v=ΔtΔs​=8−0128−0​=16 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1
The instantaneous velocity when t=2t = 2t=2 and when t=6t = 6t=6 is:
vt=2=40−06−1=8v_{t=2} = \frac{40 - 0}{6 - 1} = 8vt=2​=6−140−0​=8 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1
vt=6=120−08−3=24v_{t=6} = \frac{120 - 0}{8 - 3} = 24vt=6​=8−3120−0​=24 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1
average 16 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1; instantaneous 8 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1 at t = 2 s and 24 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1 at t = 6 s

Analysing motion through graphs
d Explain the difference between instantaneous speed and average speed. Use the graph above to help you to highlight the difference between the two. (4 marks)

Working

Instantaneous speed is the speed that a body is moving at a particular moment in time (1 mark), while average speed is the speed that a body would have to maintain to travel the same distance as the distance covered in the trip (1 mark). For example, at 4 seconds the car has an instantaneous speed of 20 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1 (1 mark) but throughout the journey the car has an average velocity of vavg=st=15025=6v_{avg} = \frac{s}{t} = \frac{150}{25} = 6vavg​=ts​=25150​=6 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1 (1 mark).

You tryWorksheet 7B–1 Analysing motion through graphs Q6

Analysing motion through graphs
What is the difference between the average velocity and the instantaneous velocity? Give an example to support your answer. (4 marks)

Working

The average velocity of an object is the change in the displacement of an object divided by the time. (1 mark)
The instantaneous velocity of an object is the velocity of an object at a specific point in time. (1 mark)
For example, if a hiker walks 5 km in an hour, the magnitude of their average velocity would be 5 km h−1\text{km h}^{-1}km h−1. (1 mark)
However, in their hike the hiker may have run, walked or stopped and rested in sections
at any given instant their velocity can be different. (1 mark)
